summary: Specifies the minimum set of core attributes for a white pages entry describing a person, and how new object types using those attributes can be defined and published. It aims to make directories of people searchable in a common way.

eli5.summary: It is an agreement about what a phone-book entry for a person should contain, so different phone books can be read the same way.

subtitle: A minimum, implementation-neutral list of fields that every Internet phone-book entry for a person should have.

tldr.problem: Different White Pages servers describe people differently, so users and developers cannot expect the same kinds of information from each service.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Person Information Object Template: a flat list of core attributes with recommended maximum sizes and syntaxes, plus rules for publishing new templates.
tldr.outcome: Conforming implementations must support the core attributes, and each technology (WHOIS++, LDAP, vCard and others) publishes its own companion mapping. It is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Multivalued attributes
facts.value: Email, Certificate, Common Name, Language Spoken

today: RFC 2218 is a Proposed Standard published in October 1997, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Common Person Object
sections.content:
The Internet community stated a need for a White Pages service for finding information about people. For the Internet White Pages Service (IWPS) to interoperate and feel the same to users, every person must have a common set of information.

A common user object lets a user move between implementations and expect the same kinds of information. It also gives developers one unambiguous way to represent what the service manages.
sections.eli5: If every phone book lists the same basic things about each person, you never have to relearn how to read a new one.

sections.title: Scope and What Is Left Out
sections.content:
The document sets the attributes of the Common User Information Object. It is not an exhaustive list of everything the IWPS could store, but the process it uses is recommended for defining other objects.

All conforming implementations must support at least the core attributes. They may add local attributes and still conform.

Three things are explicitly out of scope: rules on information privacy (each country has its own laws), a directory access protocol such as whois++, LDAP or DAP, and the database structure. The database structure could restrict implementations (an X.500-based schema versus a DNS-based one), so it is left as a separate research topic.
sections.eli5: The rules say which boxes every entry must have. They do not say how the phone book is stored or who may look at it.

sections.title: The Person Template
sections.content:
The Person Object is a simple list of attributes. No structure and no object inheritance is implied. Storage is a local issue, so the memo suggests storage sizes but not storage types, and it does not say how a user interface should display the attributes.

The attributes fall into four groups:

  • General: Email, Cert, Home Page, Common Name, Given Name, Surname, Organization, Locality, Country and Language Spoken.
  • Personal: phone, fax, mobile phone, pager, postal address and Description.
  • Organizational: Title and the office phone, fax, mobile phone, pager and postal address.
  • Ancillary: Creation Date, Creator Name, Modified Date and Modifier Name.

Email address, Certificate, Common Name and Language Spoken are multivalued. Phone numbers should preferably be in full international form, such as +1 206 703 0852, and may carry extra text such as an extension. Multiple-line text such as an address must use the header-folding procedure of RFC 822.

These attributes describe kinds of information, not fields in any particular schema. Each technology that deploys a White Pages service must publish a companion document showing how it expresses them.
sections.eli5: An entry is a simple form with boxes for name, email, phone, address and so on. Some boxes, like email, can be filled in more than once.

sections.title: Sizes and Syntaxes
sections.content:
Clients should treat the listed sizes as maximums, counted in characters rather than bytes, but should still cope with larger values from servers that do not follow the recommendations. For example: Email 360, Cert 4000, Common Name 64, Given Name and Surname 48 each, Country 2 (ISO 3166), and postal addresses 255.

The syntaxes follow LDAP usage:

  • WhitepageString must encode arbitrary ISO 10646 characters; UTF-8 is one such encoding.
  • PrintableString is limited to letters, digits and a few punctuation marks.
  • GeneralizedTime is a printable string such as 199412161032Z. The time zone must be given, and Zulu is strongly recommended.
  • Mailbox must distinguish kinds of mailbox (for example X.400 and Internet) and be able to represent any type.
  • Address must hold at least 6 lines of 40 characters.
  • Certificate holds any kind of certificate, with X.509 as one example.
sections.eli5: Each box has a maximum length and a rule about what you can write in it, like a form that gives you only so many squares for your name.

sections.title: Publishing Templates and Keeping Data Fresh
sections.content:
The working group recommends that all information object templates used for the IWPS be published. An organization may define local templates, but any information it wants to be part of the IWPS must use a published template.

The four Ancillary attributes record who created an entry and when, and who last modified it and when. They let users judge the quality and freshness of what they retrieve. The IWPS User Agent must be able to retrieve and display them, though servers may decide whether to store them. They are recommended as the minimum set for any new template.

The motivation, quoted from RFC 1107, is that a White Pages service will not be used if its information is out of date or incorrect, so a production provider must keep data reasonably correct and current.
sections.eli5: Every entry says who wrote it and when it was last changed, so you can tell if it is old.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
Each country, and each US state, has its own privacy law. The suggested attributes may be considered private, so a directory administrator is strongly advised to check the legislation for the domain.

Following RFC 1355, each directory provider should state the purpose of the directory, what it contains and the privacy policy for that information, including limits on dissemination. This is strongly recommended for the US and Canada and required by many countries in the European Community for data sharing.

Security is implementation and deployment specific and is not addressed, except that security must make sure the privacy constraints are met.
sections.eli5: A phone book holds personal details, so whoever runs it should say what it is for and follow the local privacy rules.
